tagline: A mining toll road became a public crossing of Yosemite’s high country
intro: Tioga Road winds on two lanes through lodgepole pine, red fir and Yosemite’s subalpine high country. Tioga Road/Big Oak Flat Road carries National Scenic Byway and National Forest Scenic Byway designations. Granite overlooks, Tenaya Lake and Tuolumne Meadows mark the climb toward 9,945-foot Tioga Pass, California’s highest highway pass. The National Park Service describes Tioga as a seasonal crossing, typically open from late May or June into November.

The two roads have different beginnings. Big Oak Flat Road grew from a Gold Rush pack trail into a wagon road reaching Yosemite Valley in 1874. Tioga Road was built in 1883 to reach silver mines east of the pass and became a private toll road. In 1915, Stephen Mather purchased it with personal funds and donations from the Sierra Club and Modesto Chamber of Commerce, enabling public passage through the high country.

From the Big Oak Flat entrance, follow the road to Crane Flat, where Tioga Road branches east. Forest gives way to the overlook at Olmsted Point; the road descends to Tenaya Lake, then climbs again toward Tuolumne Meadows. Beyond the meadows, Dana Meadows leads to Tioga Pass at the park’s eastern boundary. Continuing east means a separate descent through Lee Vining Canyon to US 395.

moments.title: Olmsted Point
moments.text: Olmsted Point looks south into Tenaya Canyon toward the northern side of Half Dome and Clouds Rest, with Tenaya Lake to the east. Boulders left by glaciers scatter the granite slopes beside the parking lot. A short trail passes through trees to a small granite dome with clearer views of Half Dome and Clouds Rest. Snow still shapes road work here: before spring plowing, the park’s avalanche crew assesses the Olmsted Point zone. The National Park Service says this avalanche zone commonly remains active into the middle or latter part of spring.

moments.title: Tenaya Lake
moments.text: Tenaya Lake occupies a glacial basin backed by light granite rock, at an elevation of 8,150 feet. The Tenaya Glacier flowed here from the Tuolumne Ice Sheet toward Yosemite Valley. The glacier carried little debris and left few deposits near the lake. Water continues along that connection: Tenaya Creek serves as the lake’s principal inlet and outlet, then runs through Tenaya Canyon into the valley. The lake lies beside the Tioga Road, between Olmsted Point and the climb to Tuolumne Meadows. Trails from the lake lead toward Cathedral Lakes, Clouds Rest, Half Dome and the Yosemite Valley floor.

moments.title: Tuolumne Meadows
moments.text: Shallow groundwater sustains the meadow vegetation beside the Tuolumne River. Snowmelt and water from hillside aquifers feed the river and its creeks. The vegetation changes with landform and summer water-table depth: seasonally flooded ground supports inflated sedge and Sierra willow, while lodgepole pine grows on drier uplands and meadow edges. The Civilian Conservation Corps laid out the road’s present route through the meadows in the 1930s. Above this low ground are views of the Cathedral Range and Unicorn Peak to the south, and Lembert Dome and Mount Dana to the east.

practical: Tuolumne Meadows: Tioga Road closes to vehicles for winter. NPS gives its typical vehicle season as late May or June until sometime in November. (checked 2026-10-11)
